## Timing Is a State Question, Not Just a Clock Question {#sec-lay-ch22}

## A Concrete Picture

A cook watches both the timer and the bread. Twelve minutes specifies elapsed
time; temperature and structure describe what has happened during it. Neither
one thermometer reading nor a timer reveals the entire loaf's condition.

The same distinction matters in a swing. A wrist command applied 100 ms after
transition can encounter different club angles, velocities, shaft deflections
and existing loads. Triggering at one club angle removes that particular angle
difference, but the other quantities can still differ. The useful question is
which information predicts a feasible opportunity to improve the chosen outcome.

![Schematic Clock and Coordinate Triggers for Three Artificial Trajectories: Equal Coordinate Values Can Occur at Different Times and Rates.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_clock_vs_state.svg){#fig-lay-clock-state width=97% fig-alt="Three artificial scalar trajectories have different offsets and rates. A fixed clock line intersects different coordinate values; threshold markers share one coordinate value but have different times and slopes. These are not complete swing states or measured trajectories."}

## How the Mechanism Works

### Specify What Reaches the Trigger

Let $x$ contain every state needed to predict the declared model: positions,
velocities, actuator states, elastic memory and any controller memory. A measured
quantity is generally only a function of that state. A club-angle threshold,
for example, does not specify bilateral hand force, shaft strain or activation.
Even identical poses can have different futures.

Define an event by a scalar function $g(x,t)=0$, then specify which root counts.
One useful rule is the first upward crossing after a registered transition,
inside a declared admissible region. An unsigned equality alone also admits
backward crossings, repeated crossings and tangential touches. Define what
happens if no admissible event occurs before the horizon. Noise suppression,
hysteresis and a one-shot latch change the policy and must be included in it.

An event detector also has numerical limits. A solver that searches for sign
changes between integration steps can miss multiple crossings inside one step;
a tangential touch need not change sign. Event localization and step-size
sensitivity therefore need their own checks. A small differential-equation
residual is not proof that the intended event was found.

The figure uses three invented scalar curves. It illustrates the two timing
rules, not an advantage of one controller. Their threshold values agree while
their slopes differ; no claim of full-state matching follows.

### A Slow Crossing Magnifies Timing Error

For smooth pre-event motion $\dot x=f(x,t)$, the rate of change of the event
function is

$$
\dot g=g_t+\nabla_xg\cdot f.
$$

A *transverse* crossing has $\dot g\ne0$. If a small perturbation changes the
event-function value at the nominal event time by $\delta g$, first-order
implicit differentiation gives

$$
\delta t_e\approx-\frac{\delta g}{g_t+\nabla_xg\cdot f}.
$$

Evaluate the denominator on the approach side if detection switches the control
law. The numerator can include a threshold error or the changed trajectory's
state error at the original event time. This is a local approximation for the
same identifiable crossing, not a rule for arbitrary event changes.

For a manufactured angle crossing, a positive 0.002 rad error shifts detection
about 0.5 ms earlier at 4 rad/s, but 50 ms earlier at 0.04 rad/s. The latter
calculation is exact for a linear angle trace; a curved trace over that longer
interval needs explicit root evaluation. At a grazing event the denominator
vanishes. In dimensionless time $s$, the example
$g=(s-0.2)^2+\epsilon$ has no real event for positive $\epsilon$, two for negative
$\epsilon$, and a double root at $s=0.2$ when $\epsilon=0$. A confidence interval around one assumed
time cannot describe all three possibilities.

Report missed and multiple events as outcomes. Add synchronization error,
processing delay and uncertainty in the observable proxy. A timestamp reported
to a millisecond need not be accurate to a millisecond.

### Separate the Command From the Torque Response

Command onset, transmitted torque, contact wrench, acceleration, a velocity
peak and delivery are distinct events. An ideal command step produces an
instantaneous torque step only in a model that directly equates command and
applied torque. A finite step in torque still does not instantaneously change
velocity in a smooth mechanical system.

For an illustrative first-order torque response $a$ to a constant target $u$,
with time constant $T_a>0$,

$$
\dot a=\frac{u-a}{T_a},\qquad
 a(t)=u+(a_0-u)e^{-t/T_a}.
$$

Time is measured from the target change and $a_0$ is the existing torque state.
With zero initial output and a unit target, the response reaches about 63.2%
after one time constant. Its 10--90% rise time is $T_a\ln9$. Thus a **35 ms time
constant means approximately 76.9 ms of 10--90% rise**, not 35 ms of rise.
A pure delay postpones the response; it is a different parameter.

Initial load matters as well. For a target change from $-5$ to $+15$ N m and
$T_a=35$ ms, the existing output remains $-5$ N m at the change, crosses zero
after $T_a\ln(4/3)\approx10.1$ ms, and approaches $+15$ N m gradually. These
are manufactured actuator examples, not measured muscle timings. Rate limits,
saturation, contact changes and elastic transmission can change this response.
A preloaded channel can already carry force without responding instantaneously
to a new target.

Compare step, ramp and filtered commands with declared initial actuator states
and capacities. Equal targets and nominal onset do not guarantee equal torque
impulse, mechanical work or load. Work requires the applied torque paired with
its conjugate rate, as in @sec-lay-ch13. To test how preparation established a
load, include that history and its cost. To test a subsequent intervention,
copy the complete prepared state before branching. Those are different questions.

### What the Recorded Timing Studies Establish

The pinned [two-link methods](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/85cce4d3307bb7ad3953d9fc6e583e370803515c/docs/research/proximal_distal_energy_transfer/chapters/_ch06_methods.qmd)
use a fixed hub, rigid club, projected gravity and retained joint damping.
They compare constant shoulder commands of 60 or 100 N m with zero wrist drive,
drive-only, or restrain-then-drive programs. The positive wrist target is 15 N m, with early restraint magnitudes of 5 or
10 N m where included. Fifteen onset values from 0 to 0.35 s, separated by
25 ms, form 92 attempted programs across the two shoulder levels. The
zero-wrist-command condition retains the model's damping; it is not necessarily
a torque-free anatomical wrist. Constant shoulder command also does not mean
equal shoulder work when the angular trajectories differ.

The endpoint is the first upward crossing of the club's absolute angle through
zero, scored only if the arm angle is at most 2 rad. It is a registered geometric
delivery proxy, **not a simulated ball collision**. In the unfiltered sweep,
63 of 92 programs satisfy that rule. Excluded crossings remain recorded. A
schedule that fails the rule cannot quietly disappear from the denominator or
be compared at a later, more favorable crossing.

The [command-filter audit](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/85cce4d3307bb7ad3953d9fc6e583e370803515c/scripts/research/proximal_distal_energy/e1e_smooth_command_sensitivity.py)
repeats the grid at time constants of 0, 20, 35 and 50 ms. Its implementation
copies the initial command directly into the filter state and smooths subsequent
changes. This is a declared preloaded initialization; it does not simulate the
process that established that initial torque.

Across these four settings and both shoulder levels, the four comparison speeds increase
from early drive (onset at zero) through zero wrist command and grid-selected
drive-only to grid-selected
restrain-then-drive. The selected onset is allowed to change with the filter.
At 60 N m, the selected drive-only onset moves from 0.200 s without filtering to
0.175 s at 35 ms. Accepted counts change too: 63, 59, 59 and 56 out of 92 as the
time constant increases. These are stored finite-grid results, not a continuous
optimum, one fixed policy succeeding everywhere, or human timing prescriptions.


A [separate uncertainty comparison](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/85cce4d3307bb7ad3953d9fc6e583e370803515c/docs/research/proximal_distal_energy_transfer/chapters/_ch06d_uncertainty_control.qmd)
uses moving-base, two-hand, flexible-club dynamics, delayed bounded actuators,
eight schedules and six held-out parameter draws. Its nominal wrist targets differ: `early_restrain` requests -2 N m before
0.10 s and +4 N m afterward; `late_drive` requests zero before 0.14 s and
+5 N m afterward. Delivered drive remains subject to delay, lag and bounds.
This comparison changes early torque, switching time and late amplitude; it
does not isolate early restraint alone. The named `early_restrain` schedule improves
the sampled 10th-percentile speed relative to `late_drive` while worsening mean
planar face/path error. All eight schedules are nondominated across five
objectives: that speed quantile, mean face/path error, upper-tail hand force,
squared-torque effort and speed dispersion. The last four are minimized; the
speed quantile is maximized. This describes tradeoffs among the sampled
schedules, not a proven boundary of every feasible policy.
Its endpoint is the fixed time 0.24 s, not the preceding study's crossing.
Neither comparison tests a general advantage of observable state feedback over
clock schedules, and the engineering draws are not a golfer population sample.

Sprigings and MacKenzie separately compared three optimized conditions in a
planar torso--arm--club model with constrained torque generators. They reported
a small advantage from resisted delay and an advantage from active wrist torque
after release [@sprigings2002]. That published simulation supports a bounded
model question, not an identified human command history or the parameters of
our separate filter audit.

**Model Result:** Selected timing and speed rankings depend on the model,
candidate family, initialization and endpoint. The recorded filter comparisons
retain their stated ordering within those boundaries.

**Human Evidence:** The simulations above do not measure human command onset,
preactivation or a physiological delay. Kinematics and EMG are different
observations; neither alone identifies the complete transmitted wrench history.

**Hypothesis:** Preparation can arrange geometry, motion and loading so that a
later distal action becomes useful. An observable event might select that
opportunity more reliably than a fixed clock, but this requires a prospective
comparison with delays, failures and competing objectives included.

**Practical Interpretation:** Define what “late” is relative to, which signal is
available, and what outcome improves before turning it into a cue.

### Alignment Changes the View, and Sometimes the Units

Subtracting impact time from every timestamp translates a trial's time axis;
it does not stretch the trial. Scaling each downswing to a common percentage
is an additional operation. With duration $D=t_{\mathrm{end}}-t_0>0$ and phase
$\phi=(t-t_0)/D$, corresponding phase values can still contain different states.
For an angular coordinate $q$, the derivative $dq/d\phi=D\dot q$ has units
of radians per unit phase, not rad/s.

For physical power $P$, preserve the time Jacobian when computing work:

$$
W=\int_{t_0}^{t_{\mathrm{end}}}P(t)\,dt
 =D\int_0^1P(t_0+D\phi)\,d\phi.
$$

Two manufactured traces with the same displayed curve $P=10+5\phi$ W but
durations 0.2 and 0.4 s deliver 2.5 and 5 J. Their identical phase plots do not
imply identical work. A nonlinear time warp needs its local $dt/d\phi$, and
averaging before integration need not reproduce the mean of trial work.

An event used to align curves will be sharp at the alignment origin by
construction. Greater sharpness after state alignment does not, by itself,
show a causal mechanism. Publish physical time, absolute duration, the alignment
rule and uncertainty alongside phase plots. Compare proposed explanations on
independent outcomes rather than rewarding the feature used to align them.

### A Real-Time Policy Cannot Know Future Impact

Retrospective “100 ms before actual impact” is available after the trial. A
controller cannot use that future timestamp directly. It can use a prediction
from present and past observations, with an explicitly evaluated prediction
error. The same restriction applies to normalized phase if its denominator uses
the future downswing duration.

An open-loop schedule chooses commands from elapsed time and declared initial
conditions. A state-triggered rule uses available state estimates and detector
memory. Elapsed time can itself be included in an augmented mathematical state;
that formal conversion does not give a clock schedule information about an
unobserved deviation.

For a fair comparison, declare the sensor set, sampling, latency, estimator,
actuator bounds, training data and available preparation. A trigger based on an
unmeasured shaft mode or an engine's internal force decomposition is initially
a simulation diagnostic. Its experimental proxy needs validation. Robustness of
an ideal full-state controller does not establish robustness of a delayed
measurement-based implementation, much less a complete neural controller.

### Test Preparation, Causation and a Usable Timing Region

A moment's sign crossing is not necessarily the beginning of the physical
interaction: the same channel may have acted earlier with the other sign.
A later action cannot alter the physical past, but measured event order alone
does not isolate the cause of a state change. Sensor delays, filtering, shared
state dependence and opposing contributions complicate that inference.
Specify the body, moment point and projection axis before comparing couple
onsets; pair power channels with their own conjugate velocities.

Compare forward branches from a complete copied state to ask what removing or
changing a declared input does next. Each branch must evolve its own reactions
and reach the registered endpoint, or report failure. A separate preparation
experiment should account for how different states were reached. Reoptimizing
other controls after removal asks whether another strategy can substitute; it
does not estimate the same fixed-policy effect.

Continuous arm loading and phase-dependent redistribution between arm and wrist
channels remain candidate explanations. A change of allocation need not produce
a net torque sign reversal, and an unchanged net sign can hide large internal
changes. Relate the predictions to bilateral loads, stored energy, work and
estimated stiffness, rather than treating one onset as a biological role label.
A changed mediator consistent with a cue is informative but does not by itself
establish mediation: competing pathways and confounding still need a design.

There may be a broad useful region, a narrow peak, a boundary solution, several
separated regions or no feasible benefit. Search and report the actual response
surface under declared speed, direction and load requirements. A plateau is a
result to establish, not a consequence of calling timing robust. Include onset
jitter, measurement error, event failure and held-out uncertainty. If the proposed
region is narrower than the experiment can resolve, do not claim that the
experiment has located it precisely.

### Reader Lab: Audit One Proposed Timing Rule

First reproduce the filter's 63.2% response, 76.9 ms rise interval and 10.1 ms
sign-reversal example. Then compare the crossing rates of 4 and 0.04 rad/s and identify where the
local timing approximation breaks. Finally integrate the phase power traces
with their actual durations. These exercises separate actuator history, event
uncertainty and energy accounting.

For a proposed swing rule, freeze the event definition and training choices
before testing. Compare clock and observable-event policies on the same declared
task and information budget. Report all attempted trials, event ambiguity,
failures, latency, complete outcome distributions and uncertainty, rather than
only the successful mean. Include raw-time and phase views with reproducible
detection code. A prospective performance comparison is stronger evidence than
a sharper aligned plot.

## Where the Picture Breaks

An oven's few visible indicators make the analogy attractive; a golfer's
relevant internal state is much less accessible. One angle can be a useful
predictor without being either a complete state or the cause of a favorable
outcome. A simulated trigger can also exploit measurements and response times
that an experiment cannot provide.

Preparation determines the state available for a later action. Event detection
determines when the policy recognizes it. Actuator dynamics determine what load
actually changes before the task ends. Their interaction, together with the
objective and feasible constraints, is the timing question.
